title: Search Underway After Air Ambulance Flying Bermuda to Boston Loses Contact Off Nantucket
excerpt: Air traffic control audio indicates the C-GRJP pilot reported electrical problems and told controllers the aircraft was 'coming in blind' before descending from approximately 24,000 feet as a storm approached. Latest confirmed details and expert analysis.
summary: A Canadian-registered air ambulance with six people on board that departed Bermuda early Saturday morning has disappeared from radar off the coast of Massachusetts, prompting an active search and resc
body:
UPDATE — C-GRJP's Final Moments

C-GRJP pilot reportedly told air traffic control the plane was 'coming in blind'

Electrical problems reported before aircraft descended from approximately 24,000 feet as storm approached

New details from air traffic control audio and preliminary flight-tracking data are providing additional insight into the final moments of missing medical transport aircraft C-GRJP.

The Gulfstream G100 was travelling from Bermuda to Boston when contact was lost early Saturday morning. Air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net indicates the pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the aircraft approached the Massachusetts coast.

In one exchange, a controller can be heard asking: "Roger, you said you're coming in blind. Is that what you said?"

Preliminary Flightradar24 data also indicated the aircraft descended from its cruising altitude of approximately 24,000 feet to around 10,000 feet.

Former U.S. Department of Transportation Inspector General and aviation attorney Mary Schiavo said the available information raised the possibility that the aircraft had lost navigational instruments while encountering deteriorating weather conditions.

Schiavo also warned that loss of instruments can leave pilots vulnerable to spatial disorientation, particularly when flying in poor visibility.

However, the cause of the incident has not been determined, and Schiavo's comments represent analysis of the limited information currently available — not an official finding by investigators.

The aircraft was carrying four Canadian crew members and two Bermudian passengers when it departed L.F. Wade International Airport for Boston.

A debris field associated with C-GRJP was subsequently located off Nantucket.

Bermuda Observer will continue updating this page as confirmed information becomes available.

UPDATE — October 5, 2026

Police Identify the Two Bermudians Aboard C-GRJP

The Bermuda Police Service has officially confirmed the identities of the two Bermudian nationals who were aboard the air ambulance that went missing off Nantucket Island shortly after 1:00 a.m. on Saturday, October 3, 2026: 66-year-old Marilyn Lavonne Bean and her 41-year-old son, Sergio Wayne Lottimore.

A police spokesperson said: “The Bermuda Police Service [BPS] can now confirm the identities of the two Bermudian Nationals who were on board an aircraft which went missing just off Nantucket Island, Massachusetts, U.S.A., shortly after 1:00 a.m. on Saturday, October 3, 2026, as 66-year-old Marilyn Lavonne Bean and her 41-year-old son, Sergio Wayne Lottimore.

“The investigation into this incident is being conducted by the U.S. National Transportation and Safety Board, in conjunction with Transport Safety Board, Canada.

“A BPS Family Liaison Officer has been appointed to assist the relatives of Ms. Bean and Mr. Lottimore, during this difficult time.

“The BPS extends its sincere condolences.”

The confirmation means that of the six people aboard the Gulfstream G100, two — Ms. Bean and her son — were Bermudian. The four other people on board were Canadian nationals. Families on both sides of the Atlantic have now been formally notified.

UPDATE — October 4, 2026 (Evening)

The U.S. Coast Guard suspended active search operations at approximately 7:00 p.m. on Sunday, October 4, after continuous searching by air and sea assets failed to locate the six people who were aboard C-GRJP. In a statement, the agency expressed its deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those on board.

Debris Field Located 20 Miles Off Nantucket

Searchers recovered debris from the medical flight in waters between 80 and 90 feet deep, roughly 20 miles off the Nantucket coast. Rear Admiral Matt Lake, Commander of the Coast Guard's Northeast District, said crews covered more than 2,840 square miles of ocean during the two-day operation. Officials described the debris as extensive but said the volume of wreckage makes immediate identification difficult. The aircraft's flight recorder had not been located — and because C-GRJP was operating as a medical transport, it was not required to carry the same cockpit recorders as a commercial airliner.

Four Canadians, Two Bermudians Aboard

The Coast Guard confirmed the six people on board were four Canadian citizens and two Bermuda citizens. Officials said they have been in contact with the families. The Government of Bermuda has asked that the privacy of the families be respected.

Aviation Analyst: “They Were Coming in Blind”

Mary Schiavo, former U.S. Department of Transportation Inspector General, told U.S. media that radar records and limited cockpit communications indicate the crew had lost their navigation instruments. Tracking data shows the aircraft dropped from approximately 24,000 feet toward 10,000 feet — a profile consistent with a loss of cabin pressure or a serious electrical fault, possibly involving heat or fire — and that the aircraft made twenty or more circling or triangular turns before disappearing. That pattern, Schiavo said, points to one of two scenarios: spatial disorientation of the pilot in deteriorating weather, or a mechanical failure that prevented the aircraft from responding to control inputs. Both, she noted, would have presented the crew with an extremely dangerous situation.

What Happens Next

With the active search suspended, the investigation shifts to recovery and analysis of the debris field. The Bermuda Observer will continue to update this page as confirmed information becomes available.

A Canadian-registered air ambulance with six people on board that departed Bermuda early Saturday morning has disappeared from radar off the coast of Massachusetts, prompting an active search and rescue operation by the U.S. Coast Guard.

The aircraft was en route from Bermuda to Boston when air traffic controllers lost contact early Saturday.

UPDATE — October 3, 2026

Since this report was published, additional information has emerged about the final stages of HTT104’s Bermuda-to-Boston flight.

Flight-tracking data indicates that C-GRJP descended rapidly from approximately 24,000 feet to around 11,000 feet before appearing to level off. The crew also reportedly declared an emergency, with an electrical issue reported before contact with the aircraft was lost.

Aviation experts are examining the rapid descent and weather conditions along the route, but the official cause of the disappearance has NOT been determined.

Regarding the 15-minute Hamilton flight covered in the video above: flight-tracking records confirm that the aircraft departed Hamilton, Ontario, and returned to Hamilton approximately 15 minutes later on October 1. The purpose of that flight remains unconfirmed. There is currently no established evidence that it was a maintenance/test flight or that it was connected to the later electrical problem.

The U.S. Coast Guard search for the aircraft and the six people aboard remains the priority.

Government Confirms

The Government of Bermuda confirms that an air ambulance which departed Bermuda for Boston early this morning, carrying six people, has been reported missing after contact was lost with air traffic control.

The United States Coast Guard is conducting search and rescue operations off the coast of Nantucket, Massachusetts. The Government has been in contact with the families of those on board and remains in contact with the overseas authorities coordinating the search.

Premier David Burt said, “My thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time. We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts.”

The Government asks that the privacy of the families be respected and will provide further updates as confirmed information becomes available.

What Skyport Has Confirmed

Skyport, operator of L.F. Wade International Airport, has confirmed the departure:

A Canadian-registered air ambulance departed L.F. Wade International Airport for Boston at approximately 12:41 a.m. on Saturday, October 3, 2026, with six souls on board, including four crew members and two passengers.

The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration has advised that air traffic controllers subsequently lost contact with the aircraft off the coast of Nantucket Island, Massachusetts, and a search is currently underway. Skyport has no further information to provide at this time.

The 12:41 a.m. departure time reported by Skyport aligns with earlier aviation reports listing the departure as approximately 11:41 p.m. Friday night.

Search Operation

The U.S. Coast Guard says it has deployed both air and surface crews to search for the aircraft. Operations are concentrated in waters south of Nantucket, Massachusetts.

The FAA has advised that contact was lost during the early hours of Saturday. The Coast Guard operation remains an active search and rescue mission.

The Aircraft

Reports identify the aircraft as a Gulfstream G100, a twin-engine business jet, registration C-GRJP. The aircraft in the file photo above shows that registration, with a Canadian flag and air ambulance markings on the tail.

American media and aviation observers are reporting the aircraft was operating as HTT104 on the Bermuda to Boston Logan International Airport route, and is operated by Latitude Air Ambulance, a Hamilton, Ontario-based medical aviation company. Latitude's Director of Flight Operations, Clarence Togeretz, is quoted in those reports as saying the aircraft had been carrying out a medical evacuation in Bermuda.

According to preliminary flight-tracking information cited by aviation observers, the aircraft descended more than 9,000 feet over a period of about 2 minutes. The last data was received approximately 2 minutes later near the current search area. That tracking data has not been confirmed by the FAA or Coast Guard.

At a Glance

Route: L.F. Wade International Airport, Bermuda to Boston Logan International Airport
Departure: Approximately 12:41 a.m. Saturday, October 3, 2026
Aircraft: Gulfstream G100 Astra SPX, reported registration C-GRJP
Operator: Reported as Latitude Air Ambulance, Hamilton, Ontario
On board: 6 souls - 4 crew, 2 passengers
Last contact: Early Saturday, off Nantucket Island
Search: U.S. Coast Guard air and surface crews, waters south of Nantucket
Identities: Not yet officially released
Cause/Status: Not yet known; authorities have not confirmed a crash

Authorities have not released the identities of those on board and have not confirmed what happened to the aircraft.

This is a developing story. The Bermuda Observer will provide updates as confirmed information becomes available from Skyport, the FAA, and the U.S. Coast Guard.

body:
Bermuda's iconic Gombey dancers brought colour, rhythm and tradition to the Botanical Gardens this afternoon as the annual Gombey Festival Showcase got underway in Paget.

The event drew together several of the island's Gombey troupes, each performing in their distinctive hand-crafted costumes adorned with vibrant capes, headdresses and masks. Accompanied by the driving beat of drums and whistles, the dancers entertained spectators with the spirited routines that have made the Gombey tradition one of Bermuda's most cherished cultural art forms.

The festival, held on October 3, offered residents and visitors alike an opportunity to experience the island's rich heritage in one of Bermuda's most picturesque settings. The Botanical Gardens provided a scenic backdrop as troupes took turns demonstrating the unique styles and choreography passed down through generations.

Gombey dancing holds deep historical significance in Bermuda, blending African, Caribbean and British influences into a performance tradition that remains a fixture at community celebrations throughout the year. Organisers say the showcase serves not only as entertainment but as a way to preserve and promote the cultural legacy for younger generations.

Those unable to attend in person were able to follow the festivities through live video coverage, with footage of the performances expected to be made available online for viewing after the event.

Former Bermuda captain David Hemp has been named head coach of Bangladesh’s women’s national cricket team, signing a two‑year deal that runs through September 2028. At 55, Hemp will join the squad in Brisbane as they prepare for a One‑Day International series against Australia.

Hemp’s appointment follows his successful stint with Bermuda, where he earned 64 caps and captained the side in international tournaments such as the ICC World Cricket League. The move comes after Bangladesh’s previous coach, Sarwar Imran, stepped down in February 2025.

title: Search Underway After Medevac Flight From Bermuda to Boston Disappears
excerpt: A medical evacuation aircraft carrying six people has gone missing after departing Bermuda bound for Boston, prompting an urgent search operation over the Atlantic.
summary: A medical evacuation aircraft carrying six people has gone missing after departing Bermuda bound for Boston, prompting an urgent search operation over the Atlantic.
body:
A medical evacuation aircraft carrying six people has gone missing after departing Bermuda bound for Boston, prompting an urgent search operation over the Atlantic.

The flight lost contact with air traffic controllers during its journey from the island, and authorities on both sides of the Atlantic have been alerted. The aircraft was reportedly transporting a patient along with medical personnel and crew when it vanished from radar.

Bermuda's emergency services are understood to be coordinating with United States Coast Guard and aviation officials as search efforts focus on the flight's expected route across open ocean. The roughly 770-mile journey between Bermuda and Boston crosses some of the most remote stretches of the western Atlantic, complicating rescue efforts.

Officials have not yet released the identities of those on board or details about the medical condition of the patient being transported. The type of aircraft and the operator involved have also not been formally confirmed.

Medevac flights are a lifeline for Bermuda residents requiring specialist treatment unavailable on the island, with patients regularly airlifted to hospitals in Boston and other US cities. The disappearance has sent shockwaves through the local community, where such flights are a familiar and essential service.

Authorities say updates will be provided as the search develops. Anyone with information is asked to contact Bermuda's Rescue Coordination Centre.

Bermuda’s Civil Aviation Authority immediately notified international aviation safety bodies, and the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration issued a search alert. Officials in Hamilton said the island’s emergency services are coordinating with U.S. agencies, and the Bermuda Search and Rescue Coordination Centre is monitoring satellite data and weather conditions that may affect search operations. The Bermuda Tourism Authority has urged visitors to stay calm and will provide updates as more information becomes available.

The disappearance has prompted a review of air‑traffic procedures over the North Atlantic, and Bermuda’s Minister of Tourism and International Trade has expressed condolences to families affected. Bermuda authorities remain hopeful that a rescue operation will locate the missing aircraft and its passengers, and they have requested the public to avoid speculation until official findings are released.

Experts say growth after loss does not mean forgetting or "getting over" someone. Instead, it can take the form of renewed appreciation for relationships, a clearer sense of purpose, or a willingness to support others facing similar pain. Many residents who have lost parents, spouses or friends describe eventually channelling their grief into volunteer work, mentorship or simply being more present with the people still in their lives.

Community advocates encourage anyone struggling with bereavement to reach out, whether to family, faith leaders or professional counselling services available on the island. The Department of Economic Development expects the revised framework to generate higher quality jobs and to better align investor activity with the island’s strategic growth priorities. A public consultation period will run through the summer, after which the revised policy will be presented to Parliament for final approval.

The outcome of this review is likely to influence Bermuda’s competitive edge as a destination for high‑net‑worth individuals and will be closely watched by both local businesses and the wider Caribbean investment community.

Forecasters note that atmospheric conditions in the vicinity of Bermuda are not favourable for reorganization, with hostile wind shear and dry air expected to keep the remnants in check as they move through the region.

While the island is not expected to face severe conditions, residents may still notice some indirect effects from the passing system. Increased cloud cover, scattered showers and gusty winds are possible over the coming days, and marine conditions around the island could become choppy at times. Small craft operators and recreational boaters are advised to monitor local forecasts and exercise caution before heading offshore.

The Bermuda Weather Service continues to monitor the remnants of Fay and will issue updates should conditions change. Officials encourage the public to stay informed through official channels, particularly during what remains an active period of the Atlantic hurricane season.

Though this system appears to pose minimal danger, emergency planners remind residents that hurricane season runs through the end of November, and preparedness remains essential. Households are encouraged to keep emergency kits stocked, review family plans and ensure important documents are secured, as conditions in the Atlantic can shift quickly during the peak months of storm activity.

The programme is designed to encourage substantial economic investment in Bermuda by offering qualifying investors the opportunity to obtain residential certificates, a measure the Government views as a tool for stimulating economic activity and attracting capital to the island. The updated 2026 policy sets out the framework under which the initiative will operate going forward.

The EIRC scheme has been a notable component of Bermuda's economic strategy, aimed at drawing high-net-worth individuals whose spending, business activity and investment can benefit the local economy. Further details of the policy's implementation are expected to be of interest to the business community, legal practitioners and prospective applicants considering Bermuda as a base for residence and investment.

The event, organised by the City of Hamilton in partnership with the Royal Bermuda Hospital, attracted more than 400 attendees from across the island.

BMA staff set up a mobile health station on Main Street, where volunteers conducted blood‑pressure checks, blood‑glucose testing and basic eye‑health assessments.  They also held a brief talk on healthy eating and the importance of regular exercise, drawing on local dietary habits and the island’s active‑lifestyle culture.

Speaking at the event, Dr. Frank L. Smith, BMA president, highlighted the association’s commitment to community outreach: "Our goal is to make preventive care accessible to everyone, especially in areas that may lack routine medical services."

The initiative follows a growing trend of professional bodies in Bermuda taking an active role in public health education.  Residents praised the BMA’s hands‑on approach, noting that many had never had a health checkup in years.

The BMA plans to return next month for a second Community Day in St. George’s, continuing its mission to promote wellbeing across the island.

A Delta Air Lines flight bound for Miami from Toronto diverted to Hamilton on Friday evening after a technical fault was detected on the aircraft. The 737‑800, operating flight DL152, was scheduled to depart at 11:45 p.m. local time but was forced to return to Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport at 12:30 a.m. after the crew reported a malfunction in the aircraft’s navigation system.

Air traffic controllers in Bermuda confirmed that the aircraft was diverted to the nearest suitable airport and that all passengers were safely on board during the maneuver. No injuries were reported and the crew followed standard emergency procedures. Passengers were provided with refreshments and information on accommodation options, as the flight was expected to remain on the island for several hours while the issue was diagnosed.

The diversion is part of a broader effort by Bermuda’s aviation authorities to ensure swift response to aircraft emergencies. The island’s airport, which is one of the few in the region capable of handling wide‑body jets, has a robust emergency response plan that was activated promptly. Bermuda International Airport officials said that the flight will be able to continue to Miami once the technical problem is resolved.

Delta Airlines has issued a statement expressing regret for the inconvenience and assures that the safety of its passengers and crew remains its top priority. The airline is coordinating with Bermuda’s aviation authorities to facilitate a smooth transition and to keep passengers informed of the flight’s status. Passengers on the flight are advised to check with airline representatives for updates and to follow any instructions from airport staff regarding lodging or rebooking.

Details surrounding the reason for Thursday's diversion were not immediately available, and the airline had not issued a public statement on the matter at the time of publication. body:
The Government has begun looking into whether Bermuda should develop its own digital identity framework, though officials stress that no final decision has been made to introduce such a system.

Minister of Economy and Labour Jason Hayward told MPs in the House of Assembly on October 2 that the initiative amounts to an exploratory exercise rather than a commitment. He was explicit that the Government has not resolved to implement a digital identity and that the current work is focused on understanding what such a framework might involve for the island.

Digital identity systems, already in use in a number of jurisdictions, allow residents to verify who they are online when accessing government services, banking and other secure transactions. For Bermuda, proponents suggest such a framework could streamline interactions with public agencies and support the island's growing fintech and digital business sectors, while critics of similar schemes elsewhere have raised questions about privacy and data protection.

Mr Hayward's remarks indicate the exploratory process will examine these considerations before any policy direction is set. The Government is expected to provide further updates to the House of Assembly as the review progresses, giving residents and businesses an opportunity to weigh in on how identification in Bermuda's digital economy should evolve.

The move comes as Bermuda prepares to welcome a wave of international teams to its pitches. The qualifiers will pit the island against other Americas nations, offering local players a chance to showcase their skills on a global stage.

BCB’s spokesperson highlighted the programme’s role in building a sustainable pipeline for future national squads. "We are committed to investing in our youth," she added, "so that the next wave of Bermudian cricketers can compete at the highest level and bring success back to our home grounds."

The search will open to players aged 12 to 18 across the island, with trials to be held in Hamilton, Paget and Sandys. Those who pass the initial screenings will join a structured training schedule that includes technical drills, analysis sessions and competitive matches.

The BCB urges parents and coaches to encourage participation and to support the next cohort of Bermudian cricketers as the island steps onto the world stage in 2027.

He then joined the clergy of St. George’s Cathedral for a morning service that celebrated the diocese’s 40th anniversary of mission work in the Caribbean.

He also met with youth volunteers from the Hamilton Youth Centre, encouraging them to pursue education and community service.

body:
The Most Rev Philip Wright, Archbishop and Primate of the Church of the Province of the West Indies, is visiting Bermuda to mark a significant milestone in the island's religious heritage — the 400th anniversary of St Mary's Church.

Archbishop Wright, who also serves as Bishop of Belize, was elected to lead the province last year. He arrived on the island accompanied by his wife, Mrs Carla Suite Wright, to take part in the commemorative events honouring four centuries of worship and community at the historic Warwick parish church.

St Mary's Church holds a special place in Bermuda's ecclesiastical history, standing as one of the island's oldest places of worship. The anniversary celebrations have drawn clergy, parishioners and community members together to reflect on the church's enduring role in the spiritual life of the island since its founding in the early 1600s.

The Archbishop's presence underscores the close ties between Bermuda's Anglican community and the wider Church of the Province of the West Indies, of which the island's Anglican churches form a part. His visit is expected to include services and gatherings connected with the anniversary programme, offering an opportunity for local worshippers to meet the province's senior church leader.

The milestone comes as heritage institutions across Bermuda continue to celebrate the island's deep colonial-era roots, with churches among the oldest surviving institutions on the island.
